planting.note: Propagate by leaf cuttings or by dividing offset rosettes in moistened propagating mix; rooting is slower than in African violets since this species grows best cool and on the dry side.

directions: Petrocosmea kerrii forms a tight, symmetrical rosette of thick, deep-green, felted leaves that lie nearly flat against the pot, giving it a sculptural quality even without flowers. In late winter to spring it sends up short stalks topped with small, violet-blue, two-lipped flowers held just above the foliage, blooming more reliably indoors than many other gesneriads. Unlike most of its relatives it prefers cooler room temperatures and slightly drier soil between waterings, so let the top of the mix dry before rewatering and avoid wetting the fuzzy leaves. Grow in a shallow pot of African-violet-style mix with a pinch of crushed limestone, in bright but indirect light away from any direct sun that would scorch the rosette.
sources: Jacksonville Gesneriad Society Petrocosmea Care Guide

planting.note: Propagate by leaf cuttings or by dividing offset rosettes; this slow-growing limestone-cliff species resents soggy soil and roots best in a lean, fast-draining mix.

directions: Petrocosmea nervosa carries broader, more deeply quilted leaves than most of its rosette-forming relatives, with conspicuous pale veining radiating out from a thick, almost woody base. Clusters of small lavender to violet flowers rise on wiry stalks a few inches above the foliage in winter and spring, a welcome bloom period when little else is flowering indoors. Like other Petrocosmea species it grows slowly and dislikes constantly wet soil, so water only once the surface has dried and keep it in bright, filtered light rather than full sun or deep shade. Because the rosette lies so flat, a shallow pan or bonsai-style pot shows off its form better than a standard deep pot.

planting.note: Pot up rooted stolon plantlets, which form readily at the tips of trailing runners much like strawberry plants, into a hanging container of African-violet-style mix.

directions: Alsobia punctata is a sprawling, stoloniferous relative of Episcia that sends out long runners tipped with small plantlets, making it easy to fill a hanging basket from a single starter plant. Its white, fringed, bell-shaped flowers are heavily speckled with maroon to purple spots inside the throat, giving the plant its common name, and appear over a long season against medium-green, slightly hairy leaves. It is coarser and more vigorous than the closely related lace-flower vine Episcia dianthiflora, tolerating somewhat brighter conditions while still preferring the same warm, evenly moist, well-drained mix. Grow in a hanging container in bright indirect light, pinch back runners to keep it full, and water whenever the top of the mix begins to dry.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or divide basal offsets into a humid, close-topped terrarium or propagating case; this Puerto Rican cliff-dweller is far less tolerant of drying out than most houseplant gesneriads.

directions: Gesneria cuneifolia forms a dense, mounding rosette of smooth, glossy, dark green leaves rarely more than a few inches across, native to rocky coastal cliffs and limestone outcrops in Puerto Rico. Small, bright red, tubular flowers are produced in loose clusters almost continuously once the plant is established, held just above the foliage on short stalks. It grows best in a humid terrarium or close-topped case with constant, even moisture rather than on a normal windowsill, since it is far less forgiving of drying out than most houseplant gesneriads. Pot it in a well-drained, lime-enriched mix, keep it out of direct sun, and propagate easily from stem cuttings or by dividing offsets from the base.

planting.note: Plant small offset bulbs with their tops left exposed above the soil surface in a shallow pot of fast-draining succulent mix; covering the bulb necks invites rot.

directions: Violet Silver Squill is a compact, clump-forming bulb selection of the South African silver squill, distinguished from the plain species by the rich burgundy-violet flush on the undersides of its silver-spotted, olive-green leaves. Clusters of small, greenish flowers with purple stamens rise on slender pink stalks above the foliage in spring and summer, though the mottled, two-toned leaves remain the main attraction year-round. The small bulbs multiply readily at the soil surface and should be planted with their tops exposed rather than buried. Grow in a shallow pot of fast-draining mix in bright indirect light, and let the soil dry between waterings, especially during its winter semi-dormancy.

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings directly in moist potting mix, where they strike roots at the leaf nodes within two to three weeks; well suited to terrariums or humid trays.

directions: Exotica Purple Waffle Plant is a low, spreading selection prized for its deeply puckered, metallic leaves that are glossy purplish-green above and solid wine-red underneath, creating a shimmering two-tone groundcover effect. Small white flowers appear in short spikes in late spring but are secondary to the striking foliage, which roots wherever a trailing stem touches moist soil. It is easy in a terrarium or humid bathroom window, where its creeping habit quickly fills in as an understory groundcover beneath taller houseplants. Keep the soil evenly moist, provide bright indirect light to hold the deep purple coloring, and pinch back stems regularly to keep the mat dense rather than straggly.

planting.note: Plant the bulb with its neck at or just below the soil surface in humus-rich, free-draining soil in deep shade; keep evenly moist through the growing season and drier during winter dormancy.

directions: Dwarf Paintbrush Lily is the smallest species in its genus, producing a compact rosette of narrow, strap-like leaves topped in late summer by a tight, rounded umbel of slender, bright red to orange-red flowers only a few inches across, a miniature version of the larger paintbrush lilies in the same genus. It grows from a modest bulb native to shaded forest understory and rocky ravines along the eastern coast of South Africa, and the flower head often appears at or just above ground level before the new leaves fully expand. Plant it in humus-rich, free-draining soil in deep shade, water regularly through the growing season, and let it rest drier during winter dormancy. It is easy to raise from offsets and makes a long-lived pot subject where winters are too cold for it to stay outdoors.

planting.note: Root short stem cuttings in a loose, chunky, orchid-bark-based mix rather than dense potting soil, reflecting this species' naturally epiphytic habit.

directions: Codonanthe devosiana is a small-leaved, naturally epiphytic gesneriad from the Brazilian rainforest, trailing from a hanging pot with glossy, fleshy, closely set leaves that often show a bronzy tint on new growth. Small, white to pale lavender tubular flowers appear through the warmer months and are followed by round, berry-like orange fruit, an unusual trait among gesneriads grown as houseplants. In the wild it grows perched in mossy pockets on tree branches, so it does best in a loose, chunky, orchid-bark-based mix kept evenly moist but never waterlogged. Hang it where it gets bright, filtered light and steady humidity, and propagate new plants easily from short stem cuttings.
